items.title: Longtime Linux Developer Steps Down From Some Roles Due To Patch Flood Caused By AI
items.content:
Longtime Linux Developer Steps Down From Some Roles Due To Patch Flood Caused By AI

Written by Michael Larabel in Linux Kernel on 10 November 2026 at 07:54 AM EST. 28 Comments

Linux memory management expert Lorenzo Stoakes at Arm who has been contributing to the kernel since 2014 is stepping away from some reviewership roles within the Linux kernel due to all of the noise from the flood of kernel patches resulting fro AI/LLMs.

Lorenzo announced today he is stepping away as a reviewer for the memory management (MM), core, misc, and Rust areas due to all the noise caused by AI. Lorenzo will continue serving as maintainer for areas of the kernel he oversees but is looking to lighten his load due to the increased patch burden in 2026.

Lorenzo commented in the patch series removing himself as reviewer for those areas of the kernel:

"Given the current throughput in the kernel resulting from AI-generated series, I unfortunately lack the bandwidth to generally be able to offer review except in those areas I maintain.

I have separated the patches into areas maintained by David, Andrew, and Alice + Danilo, so each can take the patches relevant to the subsystems, for convenience.

Apologies for doing this, but given the current trends I'd like to do something to make my inbox a little more manageable :)"

Lorenzo has been a longtime contributor to the Linux memory management code and also author of the book The Linux Memory Manager.

items.title: Microsoft are rejecting your mail
items.summary: email
items.content:
On Friday morning, we became aware that a significant amount of email to Microsoft-run mail systems was being rejected. This included mail to hotmail.com and outlook.com.

The messages were being rejected with the following message:

550 5.7.1 Message rejected: Message lacks SPF/DKIM/DMARC Auth Records

We checked our logs, and found that we’d seen this message over 500 times on Thursday, but not once before that.

The affected messages all had completely valid SPF and DKIM , but did not have a DMARC record. We added a DMARC record with a “none” policy to some of the affected domains, and sure enough, mail was then accepted again. A quick fedi-survey confirmed that we were not alone.

We don’t normally re-use blog photos , but this one seemed too perfect.

DMARC records are a way of publicly stating what you want recipients to do with email that claims to be from your domain, but which doesn’t pass verification checks (DKIM or SPF) and thus is potentially forged. Your DMARC policy can be one of the following:

Publishing a policy of none is effectively the same as not publishing a policy at all.

Microsoft are now rejecting mail without a DMARC policy, but accepting mail with a policy of none . This is a massive and pointless change in their policy for incoming mail, made with no notice whatsoever.

Last year Microsoft, introduced a policy that required domains sending more than 5,000 messages per day to have a DMARC record. This change was announced in advance . This latest change appears to be completely unannounced, which makes us wonder if it was even intentional. Of course, trying to contact Microsoft in order to resolve mail issues such as this is futile.

Update: apparently it wasn’t intentional, but they haven’t figured out how to roll it back yet.

We’ve just applied p=none DMARC records to a large number of our customers’ domains. We generally try to avoid making unsolicited changes to DNS zones, but in this case we feel that it is the best option.

If you’re in contact with Microsoft users affected by this, please encourage them to complain to Microsoft; it’s very likely that they are losing other legitimate email from other providers because of this unannounced change. Better still, encourage them to move to an email provider that is pro-active in investigating email deliverability issues .

items.title: Miasma Worm Targets AI Coding Agents: 73 Microsoft Azure Repos Disabled
items.content:
An unprecedented supply chain attack bypasses registry-level scanners entirely, turning developer tools including Claude Code, Cursor, and Gemini CLI into execution vectors.

The Incident: On June 3, 2026, a highly sophisticated variant of the Miasma worm (also known as Mini Shai-Hulud) launched a coordinated, two-pronged attack targeting both the npm registry and developer source code repositories.

The Escalation: The attack successfully breached multiple high-profile GitHub accounts, including the official Microsoft Azure durabletask repository, using stolen Personal Access Tokens (PATs) and backdated commits to evade traditional audit trails.

The Response: In an ultra-rapid defensive maneuver, GitHub’s automated mitigation systems disabled 73 compromised repositories – including 49 directly associated with Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples within a mere 105-second window .

The Vector: Instead of relying on traditional package installation hooks, Miasma targets the developer’s local environment. It abuses legitimate auto-run, hook, and rule engines within modern IDEs and AI coding assistants ( VS Code, Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI ) to execute a malicious 4.3 MB staged dropper upon folder-open or agent initialization.

The Impact: Once detonated, the Bun-based worm harvests credentials for AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, npm, and GitHub, and automatically propagates by committing itself back into any repository the victim’s stolen tokens can write to.

At exactly 16:00 UTC on June 3, 2026, a silent, automated purge swept across GitHub. In a high-speed containment action lasting just 105 seconds, 73 active repositories vanished from the platform. Among them were 49 critical repositories belonging to Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples.

This drastic mitigation followed alarming telemetry indicating that threat actors behind the Miasma malware family had regained write access to key cloud repositories. The compromise exploited a stolen Personal Access Token (PAT) belonging to an active Microsoft contributor.

While security firms like StepSecurity and JFrog scrambled to document an concurrent attack vector on the npm registry where 57 malicious packages were published, a second, far more insidious arm of the campaign was already silently spreading directly inside GitHub source repositories.

By bypassing registries and package managers entirely, the Miasma worm targeted the very tools developers use to write code. It didn’t wait for npm install . Instead, it waited for the developer to simply open their code editor or launch an AI coding assistant.

The genius of the Miasma repository-poisoning campaign lies in its exploit surface. When an attacker successfully pushed malicious commits to targeted codebases (such as the popular library icflorescu/mantine-datatable ), the commits added no actual code dependencies.

Instead, the attacker checked in five innocent-looking workspace configuration files and one obfuscated JavaScript file: .github/setup.js .

│ └── settings . json < - - Claude Code SessionStart Hook

│ └── setup . mdc < - - Cursor Agent Prompt Injection

│ └── settings . json < - - Gemini CLI SessionStart Hook

│ └── tasks . json < - - VS Code Automatic Folder - Open Task

├── package . json < -- Hijacked NPM Test Script

└── setup . js < - - The 4.3 MB Staged Dropper

Each of these configuration files is designed to abuse a legitimate, developer-friendly auto-run feature within popular modern tools. Opening the cloned directory in any of these environments instantly triggers execution.

Claude Code & Gemini CLI (SessionStart Hooks)

Both Anthropic’s Claude Code and Google’s Gemini CLI support custom hooks triggered when an AI agent initializes a session in a project workspace. Miasma exploits this by defining a blanket wildcard matcher that forces the agent to execute the dropper via Node.js before any developer prompt is processed.

items.title: Australia to introduce mandatory reporting after OpenAI hack to combat artificial intelligence ‘going rogue’
items.content:
Prime minister Anthony Albanese has announced new AI safety and security protections after the OpenAI hack of Medicare. Photograph: Sarah Wilson/AAP

Prime minister Anthony Albanese has announced new AI safety and security protections after the OpenAI hack of Medicare. Photograph: Sarah Wilson/AAP

Australia to introduce mandatory reporting after OpenAI hack to combat artificial intelligence ‘going rogue’

Government flags criminal law changes to ensure companies can’t argue in future ‘that someone didn’t know the computer was loaded’

Get our daily political email , free app or daily news podcast

OpenAI will not face criminal penalties over the Medicare data breach , but the prime minister has flagged changes to Australia’s criminal law to crack down on future breaches by artificial intelligence companies.

Anthony Albanese on Tuesday released the recommendations of a “rapid review” into the June breach of a Medicare statistics reporting service portal administered by Services Australia, but not the findings or the report itself, which he committed to releasing in the future.

A key recommendation is for the Attorney-General’s Department, the Australian federal police and home affairs to consider introducing “penalties for egregious regulatory non-compliance” and a “failure to prevent” offence, which would criminalise developing an AI model that engaged in harmful conduct while failing “to take reasonable steps to prevent that harm”.

Open AI attacked Australia’s health system – and then doubled down on its negligence. The time for ‘wait and see’ is over | Kate Crawford and Edward Santow

The rapid review came in response to an AI agent, developed by OpenAI, accessing data from Services Australia and three other systems in June. The company did not notify the Australian government until mid-September despite becoming aware of the incident itself in August, prompting criticism from Labor and Albanese.

Guardian Australia revealed last month OpenAI used AI to help write the email to notify Australian authorities.

Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

Albanese said the government would set up a new AI safety regulator and implement six key obligations on AI companies:

Maintaining security controls across all stages of development and deployment.

Identifying and managing serious risks associated with their models.

Providing mandatory notification of incidents to the Australian government rapidly.

Allowing independent evaluation of their models.

Maintaining and publishing safety and security frameworks to ensure good governance, risk management and transparency.

Responding to updated standards and rules as technologies change.

The review recommended the federal government “consider mandatory, time-bound AI safety reporting”, including around AI agents behaving in ways their creators may not have intended.

Mandatory AI safety and security protections announced after OpenAI breach of Medicare – video

The home affairs minister, Tony Burke, appearing with Albanese, told reporters: “It should never be the case that there’s an argument that someone didn’t know the computer was loaded.”

“We need to make sure that our laws and our systems keep pace with the technology and also make sure that we’re able to use the technology to find vulnerabilities before others do,” Burke said.

“The mandatory reporting, when artificial intelligence goes rogue, gives us a chance to be able to make sure that when this happens, the reporting occurs and occurs immediately.”

Despite the government’s earlier public anger at OpenAI , Albanese on Tuesday characterised the company’s breach of Services Australia as “minor” in terms of the implications for personal privacy. Guardian Australia understands OpenAI is unlikely to face further legal proceedings related to the June breach.

items.title: What’s new in PHP 8.6
items.content:
PHP 8.5 has brought us features such as the pipe operator, array_first() , array_last() , the URI extension, and the #[\NoDiscard] attribute.

PHP 8.6 is shaping up to be another interesting release. It contains a mix of language improvements, new standard-library functions, better networking APIs, security improvements, and a few useful internal optimizations. It’s general availability is currently scheduled for November 19, 2026 .

So, it’s a good time to look at everything that has made it into PHP 8.6 so far.

This article is based on the features currently listed in PHP’s implemented PHP 8.6 RFCs . Some details may still change before the final release but it should largely remain the same.

Explicit endianness for pack() and unpack()

Writing to object properties referenced by constants

Deprecating return values from constructors and destructors

is_readable() and is_writable() reflection methods

The Direction-Aware Property Resolution RFC is an engine-level improvement for asymmetric properties introduced in PHP 8.4.

Asymmetric visibility lets you make a property publicly readable but restrict who can modify it:

The property can be read from outside the class, but it can only be changed inside the class.

Previously, PHP had to check the write visibility every time the property was modified. That made writes to private(set) and protected(set) properties more expensive than writes to ordinary public properties.

PHP 8.6 moves this check to the runtime-cache population phase. Once PHP knows that a particular call site has write access, subsequent writes can use the cached result.

The syntax does not change. The improvement is mostly invisible to application code, but it makes asymmetric properties cheaper to use, especially in loops, object hydration, serializers, and builders.

This is a performance improvement rather than a new language feature. Existing behavior remains the same.

Explicit endianness for pack() and unpack()

PHP 8.6 extends the format-string syntax used by pack() and unpack() .

Until now, PHP supported machine-endian signed integers, but not signed integers with an explicitly chosen byte order.

$bytes = pack ( 's<l<q<' , - 258 , - 16909060 , - 72340172838076673 );

s< — signed 16-bit little-endian integer

l< — signed 32-bit little-endian integer

q< — signed 64-bit little-endian integer

They also work with unsigned machine-endian formats:

$bytes = pack ( 'S<L>Q<' , 258 , 16909060 , 72340172838076673 );

This is particularly useful when working with binary protocols and file formats.

Existing format codes such as v , n , V , and N continue to work as before. Applying an endianness modifier to a format that already has an inherent byte order throws a ValueError .

The same syntax is also being added for floating-point values through the floating-point endianness RFC :

$bytes = pack ( 'f<d>' , 3.14159 , 2.71828 );

f< — little-endian single-precision float

d< — little-endian double-precision float

$bytes = pack ( 'f>d>' , 3.14159 , 2.71828 );

The new syntax is equivalent to the existing format letters:

pack ( 'f<' , 3.14 ) === pack ( 'g' , 3.14 );

pack ( 'f>' , 3.14 ) === pack ( 'G' , 3.14 );

pack ( 'd<' , 3.14 ) === pack ( 'e' , 3.14 );

pack ( 'd>' , 3.14 ) === pack ( 'E' , 3.14 );

PHP stream operations have historically reported errors in several different ways. Depending on the stream wrapper and operation, you might get a warning, a notice, a failed return value, or no particularly useful structured information at all.

The Stream Error Handling Improvements RFC introduces a more consistent model.

A stream context can now define how errors should be handled:

'error_mode' => StreamErrorMode :: Exception ,

StreamErrorMode::Error — use normal PHP warnings and notices

StreamErrorMode::Exception — throw exceptions for terminating errors

StreamErrorMode::Silent — suppress error output

items.content:
온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

제가 보기에는 블랙해커들 보다는 서버측이 클라이언트의 행동을 분석하는 과정처럼 보이더군요..

즐겨찾기 폴더 추가는 즐겨찾기 on 후 우측의 폴더 아이콘을 터치하여 추가할 수 있습니다.

items.title: What's new in the .NET 11 runtime
items.content:

This article describes new features in the .NET runtime for .NET 11. It was last updated for release candidate 2 (RC 2).

The minimum hardware requirements for .NET 11 have been updated to require more modern instruction sets on both x86/x64 and Arm64 architectures. Additionally, the ReadyToRun (R2R) compilation targets have been updated to take advantage of newer hardware capabilities.

For Apple, there's no change to the minimum hardware or the ReadyToRun target. The Apple M1 chips are approximately equivalent to armv8.5-a and provide support for at least the AdvSimd (NEON), CRC , DOTPROD , LSE , RCPC , RCPC2 , and RDMA instruction sets.

For Linux, there's no change to the minimum hardware. .NET continues to support devices such as Raspberry Pi that might only provide support for the AdvSimd instruction set. The ReadyToRun target has been updated to include the LSE instruction set, which might result in additional jitting overhead if you launch an application.

For Windows, the baseline is updated to require the LSE instruction set. This is required by Windows 11 and by all Arm64 CPUs officially supported by Windows 10 . Additionally, it's inline with the Arm SBSA (Server Base System Architecture) requirements. The ReadyToRun target has been updated to be armv8.2-a + RCPC , which provides support for at least AdvSimd , CRC , LSE , RCPC , and RDMA , and covers the majority of hardware officially supported.

For all three operating systems (Apple, Linux, and Windows), the baseline is updated from x86-64-v1 to x86-64-v2 . This changes the hardware from only guaranteeing CMOV , CX8 , SSE , and SSE2 to also guaranteeing CX16 , POPCNT , SSE3 , SSSE3 , SSE4.1 , and SSE4.2 . This guarantee is required by Windows 11 and by all x86/x64 CPUs officially supported on Windows 10. It includes all chips still officially supported by Intel and AMD, with the last older chips having gone out of support around 2013.

The ReadyToRun target has been updated to x86-64-v3 for Windows and Linux, which additionally includes the AVX , AVX2 , BMI1 , BMI2 , F16C , FMA , LZCNT , and MOVBE instruction sets. The ReadyToRun target for Apple remains unchanged.

Starting with .NET 11, .NET fails to run on older hardware and might print a message similar to the following:

The current CPU is missing one or more of the baseline instruction sets.

For ReadyToRun -capable assemblies, there might be additional startup overhead on some supported hardware that doesn't meet the expected support for a typical device.

.NET supports a broad range of hardware, often above and beyond the minimum hardware requirements put in place by the underlying operating system. This support adds significant complexity to the codebase, particularly for much older hardware that's unlikely to still be in use. Additionally, it defines a "lowest common denominator" that AOT targets must default to, which can, in some scenarios, lead to reduced performance.

The update to the minimum baseline was made to reduce the maintenance complexity of the codebase and to better align with the documented (and often enforced) hardware requirements of the underlying operating system.

For more information, see Minimum hardware requirements updated .

.NET 11 introduces runtime-native async (Runtime Async V2), a significant step toward replacing compiler-generated async state machines with runtime-managed suspension and resumption. Instead of the compiler emitting state-machine classes, the runtime itself tracks async execution, producing cleaner stack traces, better debuggability, and lower overhead.

Runtime Async is a preview feature. To opt in, add the following property to your project file:

A net11.0 project no longer requires <EnablePreviewFeatures>true</EnablePreviewFeatures> to use Runtime Async.

items.title: A faster Easter date function
items.summary: c++, performance
items.content:
This post is a fun little side quest to kickstart my journey optimising regional calendars.

Computing the date of Easter faster is not going to matter in any real application. Even in places where it might seem to matter, like high frequency trading applications, it is probably better to just use an in-memory lookup table for holiday dates...

However, no "Fast Date" series would be complete without some mention of this classic problem.

The rules for Easter were broadly decided at the First Council of Nicaea, organised by Emperor Constantine in 325 AD, ultimately landing on the first Sunday after the first full moon, on or after March 21 . Later, for operational efficiency, the church defined "full moon" according to a formula, which was eventually modified by Pope Gregory XIII in 1582 ("Gregorian Easter") , with the first Easter under the new rules applying in most Catholic countries the following year.

The Church of England first observed the new date of Easter in 1753, but Eastern / Orthodox churches continue to follow the old rules.

This article is about the new "Gregorian" Easter, because it is much more complex and slow to compute. For more details on the underlying algorithm, you can see Gauss's Algorithm on Wikipedia (the first known self-contained function, which basically all later algorithms build on) .

It's around twice as fast as a standard easter function that you might find in a typical date library, and I suspect it may be the fastest one made so far 🤷 .

Part of that speed is attributable to using only 5 multiplications (whereas typical reference algorithms have 10 or more multiplications) .

The accuracy range of around -11m → +16m years might seem a bit of overkill, but the reason I targeted this range is so that any date library that expresses dates via a signed or unsigned 32‑bit "rata die", is covered by this function. This means that if you decide to not clamp the logic to years after 1582, at least it will return something resembling the correct rules, rather than garbage.

Note that this function contains more terms than traditional Easter functions, but bear in mind that the compiled assembly will be a lot smaller. So if you don't care about the speed, but want a tiny impact on binary size, that could be a reason to consider this function.

The rest of this post will briefly explain the tricks used in this function:

You'll notice that the very first thing we do is add a strange value SHIFT to the input value. This is done for two reasons:

For example, most Easter algorithms have a term like (5 + 8 * c) / 25 , where c is the century ( year / 100 + 1 ). The term 25 in the calculation of shift is responsible for aligning the century such that the constant 5 can be removed, resulting in c * 8 / 25 , which is then approximated in the final algorithm with a single mul-shift: (u64) c * M25 >> 32 .

Other terms in SHIFT : 19, 400, 30 are all doing similar things related to the 19-year-cycle, 400-year-cycle, and mod-30 steps.

The term * 2 is different. Without this term, the range of coverage would be -5,403,600 → +22,363,835; which doesn't quite cover the range we wanted, which for signed 32-bit rata die, is ±5.88m years. Including * 2 increases the value of shift by exactly 5,700,000, which is how many years it takes for the Easter pattern to repeat, and gets the range we are after.

If you like this type of optimisation, but are not a fan of the low-level bit-shifting and so on, then you might prefer to use this function here below. It is a much more readable version of the function, which only has these higher-level optimisations applied.

Note that unlike in the main function presented earlier, MOD 30 needs to be a positive-modulus function (even for positive dates), and that the nextSunday helper is anchored to the internal logic of the function, not related to Unix day-counting.

Meta Hid AI Chatbot from UI (Source: X/Twitter)

Sellers are allegedly using modified Instagram builds on Android emulators like BlueStacks, then manipulating the AI with hidden characters and carefully worded prompts to force username changes. The method is reportedly being used to grab rare OG handles, including one-letter usernames, and handle-monitoring bots have already flagged several suspicious swaps.

New Instagram AI Exploit (Source: X/Twitter)

A natural language interface sitting in front of account-level APIs. No hard authentication gate before executing state changes. Someone in the audience raises their hand and says, “that’s a disaster waiting to happen.” Everyone nods.

items.title: French officials blame Iran for supermarket fridge hacking
items.content:
Stores in several countries across Europe recently experienced fridge and freezer issues Image: Elsa Rancel/Ouest-France/PHOTOPQR/MAXPPP/IMAGO Advertisement

French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said the attacks on French supermarkets last month came from Iran, and were carried out by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) , the elite branch of Iran's armed forces that answers directly to its religious leadership.

"This attack is unprecedented in both its scale and its level of aggression," Barrot said, adding "we will implement sanctions at the European level against all those responsible for this attack."

What happened during the alleged refrigeration cyberattack?

While the cyberattack was comparatively simple, it nevertheless had serious consequences for hundreds of supermarkets, spoiling large quantities of produce and in some cases setting temperatures so high that refrigeration units caught fire.

It was launched overnight on October 11-12, affecting around 700 of France's roughly 10,000 supermarkets.

The hack forced supermarkets to pull multiple products from their cold storage displays, and to throw many of them away entirely Image: Fred Tanneau/AFP

A series of similar incidents also affected French supermarkets last week , and authorities even reported a failed attempt to hack cooling units at blood banks .

Supermarkets in other European countries have reported similar security breaches, as have US authorities. It was not clear if any of all of these instances were connected.

What did French prosecutors say about the case?

Meanwhile, a Paris prosecutor provided details on the hacking probe:

"A judicial investigation has been opened against the head of the Iranian group Shahid Kaveh, an offensive cyber unit affiliated with the Electronic and Cyber Center of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, against his two deputies, and against any other individuals who may be identified," Paris prosecutor Laure Beccuau said.

Barrot's Foreign Ministry said that France "condemns in the strongest possible terms the unacceptable cyberattacks carried out on its territory by the Islamic Republic of Iran."

items.title: I deleted all my SSH keys
items.content:
I’ve been using ed25519-sk keys with YubiKeys since practically the moment they were available. But because of some specific use-cases (and because, frankly, YubiKeys are expensive) I’ve had a few traditional on-disk keys hanging around for a while just waiting for me to finally decide to get rid of them.

This post documents how I’m using various secure enclaves (YubiKey, TPM, Apple Secure Enclave) to hold/encrypt SSH key material and achieve the goal of not having any unprotected key material living on-disk.

First – Isn’t using a passphrase enough?

Probably. I don’t intend to imply that this post is the only way that anyone should be doing SSH keys. Using a passphrase will encrypt the key with bcrypt & AES which keeps it protected even if the on-disk keyfile leaks somehow.

And with a functioning ssh-agent, the passphrase should only need to be entered once per session, with the decrypted key material being held in RAM after that point.

So yes, the ’traditional’ method is probably fine for most threat models. But I’m still keen to move to hardware-backed keys anyway, mostly for the satisfaction.

When I say ‘hardware-resident’ keys, I mean keys that use a secure enclave or purpose-built hardware like YubiKeys to store or protect the key material.

The theoretical benefit here is that the hardware used to generate the SSH key is needed in order to use the key. There’s no mechanism that allows leaking or exfiltrating keys that generated using this method. Any material that does exist on-disk is useless without the hardware.

Switch to using hardware-resident keys entirely

Do so as natively as possible, avoiding additional software where I can

Test these in various real-world scenarios, such as running within an LXC or noninteractively mounting an SSHFS server

I’m going to try three different hardware methods for achieving this, which I think will cover all of my needs:

With a YubiKey (5 and newer), SSH keys can be directly enrolled into the device using ed25519-sk (where the -sk stands for “Security Key”). This doesn’t require any additional software beyond OpenSSH itself.

To store a new SSH key on a YubiKey, insert it and run:

ssh-keygen -t ed25519-sk -O resident -O application = "ssh:yournamehere" -f ~/.ssh/id_ed25519-sk

The application tag set in the command is arbitrary and can be set to whatever memorable string you prefer to differentiate between multiple SSH keys if you want to create multiple keys on the same YubiKey.

If you have ykman installed, you can now inspect the list of credentials enrolled in the device:

Credential ID RP ID Username Display name

0f41fb61... ssh:yournamehere openssh openssh

If ykman complains that you haven’t set a FIDO PIN on the YubiKey yet, you can do this with ykman fido access change-pin .

Note that you don’t actually need ykman to enrol or use SSH keys with a YubiKey but it does make managing the device more convenient.

Once the key has been created, you can retrieve the public key from disk:

sk-ssh-ed25519@openssh.com AAAAGnNrLXNzaC1lZDI1NTE5QG9wZW5zc2guY29tAAAAIA9B+2GGCkQvBzpa4WobQhfC9YU5Su3pKXBmVLSXEqfRAAAAEHNzaDp5b3VybmFtZWhlcmU= alice@hostname

This key can be used like any other SSH public key – added to authorized_keys on a host, copied with ssh-copy-id , or pasted into services that depend on SSH like Git forges.

You will also find a ~/.ssh/id_ed25519-sk file on disk (without the .pub extension). Note that although this looks like a private key, it doesn’t actually contain the key material. This is just a handle to find the relevant key on the hardware device.

To configure the key for authentication, it can be enrolled with ssh-add like a regular key, or specified directly in ~/.ssh/config :

From here, you can now SSH into the destination host as with a regular key. SSH will ask you to tap the YubiKey to confirm presence when the SSH command runs.

items.title: Next-Level Benchmarking Overfitting
items.summary: databases, performance
items.content:
blog post I remarked that database benchmarking is in a crisis

because AI agents start to overfit on individual benchmarks with

questionable techniques, which drives execution times towards zero. This

has happened with TPC-D in the past, and

broke the benchmark. TPC-H tries to fight

that with rules, but most people who publish (unofficial) TPC-H results

simply ignore the rules. In combination with overly eager AI agents,

We are seeing the next level of that with the GenDB-V system . The

corresponding paper commands “Stop Handcrafting Your Engine!

GenDB-V: Towards AI-Generated and Formally Verified Database

Systems” , and reports speedups of 22× to 61× over Umbra and DuckDB,

and all that in a fully verified system. These are indeed impressive

claims, and would suggest that traditional database engines are in

Taking a step back, though, it should be clear that a performance

improvement of a factor of 22 over Umbra is infeasible, at least if we

are talking about traditional query processing. At SF10, the 22 TPC-H

queries read roughly 15GB of (compressed) base data, and on a 9950X3D

Umbra runs all queries in a total of roughly 540ms. On that machine the

memory touched for data divided by the memory bandwidth (54GB/s) alone

is about 280ms; anything below that is infeasible. Better compression

might bring that down a bit, but not by an order of magnitude.

Unsurprisingly, the most dramatic gains of GenDB-V come from

precomputation. The agents have carefully handcrafted auxiliary data

structures for each query, which are computed at load time, and which

avoid most of the work. The physical design is heavily tuned to the

queries, too, for example, there is an extra structure that lists the

supplier rows in s_acctbal DESC order, which

makes Q2 trivial. Similar per-query data structures are

built for most queries. And we see that in the performance numbers:

Several queries already run in near-constant time at SF100: Q2 in 0.7

ms, Q17 in about 15 ms and Q4 in about 17 ms on one thread. That is the

TPC-D symptom, without stored aggregates.

There is also a “plain-array” mode, which, at first glance, is more

fair, as it avoids these excessive preparations and also reports

performance improvements of just roughly a factor of 3, which seems

achievable. But when looking closely, we see that here the agents did

something even more insane: They hard-coded

their knowledge about the data generator. They “know” that each customer

k will be at row k-1 . And they know that dbgen

numbers the i -th order 32·(i/8) + i%8 , so key

k should be at row 8·(k/32) + k%32 − 1 . Which

makes the join in query Q18 super cheap.

How does all this fit together with the claim of a fully verified

database engine? Well, the code does check if the hard-coded

knowledge about the data generator holds in practice, e.g., by checking

if the guessed join partner row is correct. If not, it falls back to a

super slow generic nested loop implementation, but as that never happens

with the official TPC-H data generator, that code path is irrelevant in

Which brings me back to my original blog post claim: Letting AI

agents optimize for a given database benchmark makes the benchmark

useless. They will do their best to find insane tricks to speed up this

particular benchmark, but none of that would work in a real system. The

high tuning and synthesis time aside, deleting a single tuple (or

inserting one in the middle) can most likely cause the whole approach to

fall off a cliff, as it forces the slow fallback path. Which is not

something you want in a production system.

Stop handcrafting your engine. Start reverse-engineering dbgen!

items.title: Zero-day exploit completely defeats default Windows 11 BitLocker protections
items.content:
A zero-day exploit circulating online allows people with physical access to a Windows 11 system to bypass default BitLocker protections and gain complete access to an encrypted drive within seconds.

The exploit, named YellowKey, was published earlier this week by a researcher who goes by the alias Nightmare-Eclipse. It reliably bypasses default Windows 11 deployments of BitLocker, the full-volume encryption protection Microsoft provides to make disk contents off-limits to anyone without the decryption key, which is stored in a secured piece of hardware known as a trusted platform module (TPM). BitLocker is a mandatory protection for many organizations, including those that contract with governments.

When one disk volume manipulates another

The core of the YellowKey exploit is a custom-made FsTx folder. Online documentation of this folder is hard to find. As explained later, the directory associated with the file fstx.dll appears to involve what Microsoft calls the transactional NTFS , which allows developers to have “transactional atomicity” for file operations in transactions with a single file, multiple files, or ones that span multiple sources.

The steps for carrying out the bypass are simple:

Copy the custom FsTx folder from the Nightmare-Eclipse exploit page to an NTFS- or FAT-formatted USB drive

Connect the USB drive to the BitLocker-protected device

Boot up the device and immediately press and hold down the [Ctrl] key

There are at least two ways to accomplish the third step. One way is to boot into Windows, hold down the [Shift] key, click on the power icon, and click restart. Another is to power on the device and restart it as soon as Windows starts booting.

In either case, a command (CMD.EXE) prompt appears. The prompt has full access to the entire drive contents, allowing an attacker to copy, modify, or delete them. In a normal Windows Recovery flow, the attacker would need to enter a BitLocker recovery key. Somehow, the YellowKey exploit bypasses this safeguard. Multiple researchers, including Kevin Beaumont and Will Dormann , have confirmed the exploit works as described here.

It’s unclear what in the custom FsTx folder causes the bypass. Dormann said that it appears to be related to Transactional NTFS, which itself uses command-log file system under the hood. Dormann further noted that by looking at the Windows fstx.dll, one will see code that explicitly looks for \System Volume Information\FsTx in the FsTxFindSessions() function.”

The contents of this FsTx directory used in the YellowKey exploit reveal no strings related to RecoverySimulation.ini. It does, however, show the files and paths \??\C:\Windows\win.ini and

\??\X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini, “where X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini is what controls what WinRE [Windows Recovery] does when it fires up.”

Dormann, who is a senior principal vulnerability analyst at Tharros Labs, continued:

But what’s intriguing to me is: Why can the presence a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume affect the contents of ANOTHER VOLUME when it’s replayed? 🤔

In a normal WinRE session, you have a X:\Windows\System32 directory that has a winpeshl.ini file in it:

However, with the YellowKey exploit, it looks like Transactional NTFS bits on a USB Drive are able to delete the winpeshl.ini file on ANOTHER DRIVE (X:). And we get a cmd.exe prompt, with bitlocker unlocked instead of the expected Windows Recovery environment. While the TPM-only Bitlocker bypass is indeed interesting, I think the buried lede here is that a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume has the ability to modify the contents of another volume when it is replayed. To me, this in and of itself sounds like a vulnerability.

A Microsoft representative declined to answer questions sent by email about the reported vulnerability other than to say the company is investigating.

items.title: UK Government 'looking seriously' at banning under-16s from Vinted and eBay
items.content:
Government 'looking seriously' at banning under-16s from Vinted and eBay

2 days ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google

Vinted and eBay could be included in the list of platforms set to be banned for children aged under 16, the culture secretary has said.

Lisa Nandy said the government was "looking seriously" at including the retailing websites in the social media ban "to keep children safe".

The UK's social media ban for under-16s is set to come into force in March next year, with children barred from accessing platforms such as Instagram, TikTok and Snapchat.

In response, eBay said it was looking forward to "understanding more and continuing to work constructively with the government". Vinted said it welcomed "open dialogue" with ministers and the regulator on the issue.

Asked on the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme whether the government was looking to ban under-16s from Vinted and eBay, Nandy said: "We are looking seriously at doing so in order to keep children safe."

It came after the Sunday Times reported that the UK's social media ban was being expanded to include the popular second-hand online marketplaces.

The move was due to fears that messaging functions on the platforms allowed strangers to groom children, according to the newspaper. It suggested similar reselling platforms, Depop and Facebook Marketplace, would also be included in the list of banned sites.

Businesses and individuals sell a host of goods on eBay, which has been a major global player in the online reselling market for years. The platform states on its website that it currently requires all of its members to be over 18 years old because listings involve "entering into a contract".

Vinted is aimed at over 18s, but its terms and conditions do allow parents or guardians to create accounts for their children, which must be used under parental supervision.

The site, on which users mostly buy and sell unwanted clothes and other fashion items, has grown rapidly recently to reach 17 million UK users.

A Vinted spokesperson said direct messaging was "part of how the platform works" but that it had a "zero tolerance for harmful or explicit content" and had moderation teams and tools to spot and remove "activity that breaks our rules".

"When we identify inappropriate behaviour, we take action, up to a permanent ban or reporting to the relevant authorities," they said.

An eBay spokesperson said the company was "focused on providing a trusted and safe marketplace experience for our millions of customers".

"While the details of the proposed legislation are not yet clear, we look forward to understanding more and continuing to work constructively with the government," they added.

The government announced it would ban under-16s accessing social media in June this year, with children prevented from accessing 10 of the biggest platforms.

YouTube will also be banned for under-16s, but YouTube Kids - a version of the video-sharing app designed to be safe for children - will not be included in the measures.

A complete list of affected platforms has not yet been released, but the government said it would cover those "whose purpose is to enable social interaction and which allow users to post material".

That means platforms that have livestreaming or features that enable the potential for strangers to contact children will also be restricted, which includes gaming sites.

It does not mean that Roblox, the biggest gaming site in the UK for those aged eight to 12, for example, will be banned for under-16s. However, certain features such as its chat function will be restricted.

But Matthew Sinclair, a senior director at the Computer and Communications Industry Association, which represents tech companies, argued that ministers should prevent the rules having "scope creep".

items.title: Agama Is Coming to Tumbleweed
items.content:
The openSUSE Project’s rolling release Tumbleweed will switch to the Agama installer before the end of the year, according to an announcement on the Factory mailing list .

Agama-based images are expected to replace the legacy YaST installer as the main download on get.opensuse.org within the coming weeks.

The project is asking users to test the new installer now and report any problems before the cutover.

Two Agama images are available to test. An offline installer with a pre-filled package cache was released late last week and can install Tumbleweed without a network connection. A network-based installer has been available for some time, but it was placed outside the standard ISO directory, so many users likely never saw this. The netinstall image is in the appliances ISO directory on download.opensuse.org , and the offline installer is at https://download.opensuse.org/tumbleweed/iso/TW-offline-installer-x86_64.iso . The traditional image remains available for now.

The switch depends on test results. Release managers will link the new images on get.opensuse.org once openQA testing and the staging workflow show the new installer is as stable as the YaST-based one. Full openQA coverage is still being built, and Agama tests are being added to the staging workflow, where the groundwork exists but the tests don’t yet run.

Less common setups are especially valuable before the cutover. These include RAID and LVM disk layouts, systems with several disks, serial console installs, offline installs and unusual hardware. Any behavior that differs from the YaST installer should be filed as a bug . Documentation is also needed, because profile-based installs and console access are not yet widely covered in guides.

The most visible change for users is that the installer no longer lets them pick individual packages. Only a curated set of patterns is offered, and not every pattern in the repository appears. The decision is a deliberate choice to simplify installation.

Tumbleweed usually adopts new technology before openSUSE’s other releases, but it held back on the installer on purpose. Leap 16.0 has used Agama since its first release, while Tumbleweed waited until the new installer either matched YaST’s features or dropped them deliberately. The project says the move is now needed because YaST is no longer under active feature development and receives only minimal maintenance. As the software it depends on keeps changing, relying on it carries growing risk. YaST, which stands for Yet another Setup Tool, was first released in April 1995.

The project plans another announcement when get.opensuse.org is ready to switch.

items.content:

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

부매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 매니저에 의해 해임될 수 있습니다.

식별 코드 기준으로 당일 글 10개, 댓글 20개 작성 시 대왕디시콘을 3일간 사용할 수 있습니다.
